To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) screening for distress in cancer patients is feasible in a busy outpatient clinic, (2) the prevalence of clinically significant distress is high, (3) patients with significant distress are more likely to have unmet supportive care needs and less likely to have received supportive care, and (4) distress screening identifies patients who are at risk of not receiving appropriate supportive care.
screening for distress in patients with cancer does not result in better outcomes than usual care.

1) the prevalence of distress in cancer patients is high, with 1 in 3 reporting high levels of psychological distress; and 2) the distress experienced by patients is not being adequately identified or managed in the clinic setting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the benefits of screening for distress in cancer patients.
the benefits of screening cancer outpatients for psychological distress, and with the benefits of providing psychosocial support for those who screen positive.
the development and evaluation of the use of a screening tool for distress in patients with cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
screening for distress is not yet recommended for routine clinical practice.
the current literature does not provide convincing evidence for the benefits of screening cancer outpatients for distress, and that further studies with appropriate design are needed.
the benefits of screening for distress in cancer patients have not yet been demonstrated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
screening for distress is feasible and acceptable in a cancer setting and that it may be useful to identify those who need additional psychosocial support.
the use of the HADS to screen for distress in patients with cancer has been shown to be feasible, valid and reliable.
we have demonstrated that a brief intervention can be delivered in a cancer centre by a nurse and that this can reduce the distress of cancer patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
screening for distress in oncology patients is not a panacea.
screening for distress in patients with cancer is feasible and acceptable, and that it can be integrated into routine clinical care.

there is a high prevalence of psychological distress in cancer patients, and that the distress levels of patients are not being adequately assessed in clinical practice.1 We are not suggesting that the use of the HADS is the ideal way to assess distress, and we are not suggesting that all cancer patients who are distressed need referral to a psychologist or psychiatrist.
